title: ML Problem Framing
summary: Learn what machine learning actually is, the four ways a model can learn, and how to decide whether a problem needs ML at all before you touch a model.

slides.markdown: **Machine learning** replaces hand-written rules with a function learned from examples. Before you touch a model, you decide three things: does this problem even need ML, what shape is the output (a label, a number, a ranking), and where the labels will come from. Get the framing wrong and no amount of tuning saves the project — this is the judgment interviewers probe hardest.

slides.subTitle: Learning a function instead of coding one
slides.markdown: Traditional software encodes a rule a human wrote: `if age > 65: senior_discount`. **Machine learning** instead learns the rule — you give it many (input, output) examples and it fits a function that generalizes to new inputs it hasn't seen. Feed a model thousands of (house features, sale price) pairs and it infers pricing patterns no one explicitly coded. The shift: you stop programming behavior and start **curating data and a training signal** instead.

slides.subTitle: Four ways to learn
slides.markdown:
Every ML problem falls into one of four learning styles, split by what training signal exists:

![The four ways a model learns: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, self-supervised](assets/ml-taxonomy.svg)

**Supervised** learns from labeled examples; **unsupervised** finds structure with no labels; **reinforcement** learns by acting for a reward; **self-supervised** manufactures its own labels from raw data (predict a masked word).

assets.alt: The four ways a model learns: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, self-supervised

slides.sectionTitle: When ML is the wrong tool
slides.markdown: ML costs data, training time, and explainability — reach for it only when rules genuinely can't be hand-written. Skip it when: the logic is **deterministic** (a tax bracket, a shipping-cost formula) — just write the `if` statements; you have **too little data** to learn a reliable pattern (a few hundred labeled examples is a rough floor for most tasks); or you need **full explainability** (a loan-denial reason a regulator can audit) and a black-box model can't give you that. A lookup table that covers every case beats a model that's 2% more "accurate" but unauditable.

slides.subTitle: Input, output, label source
slides.markdown: Turning a business ask into an ML problem means pinning down three things before writing any code: the **input** (what's available at prediction time), the **output** (what decision it drives), and **where the labels come from** (historical outcomes, human annotation, or a proxy). "Reduce churn" isn't an ML problem yet; "predict, from last-90-days usage, whether a user cancels in the next 30 days, using historical cancellations as labels" is. No label source means no training set — just a wish.

A model at training time sees only two things per example: **features** (the input signal, e.g. `login_count_7d`, `plan_type`) and the **label** (the answer you're teaching it, e.g. `churned: true`). Everything the model will ever know about the world is compressed into that feature vector — if a signal isn't captured as a feature, the model cannot use it, no matter how obvious it seems to a human. This is why feature availability **at prediction time**, not just at training time, is the real constraint.

slides.subTitle: Classification vs regression vs ranking vs clustering
slides.markdown:
Match the problem type to the shape of the answer you need — picking the wrong one wastes a training run.

| Type | Output | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Classification | discrete label | spam or not spam |
| Regression | continuous number | predicted delivery time |
| Ranking | ordered list | search results by relevance |
| Clustering | groups, no labels | customer segments |

Ask "what does the output look like" before "what model" — classification and regression are supervised, clustering is unsupervised, ranking often blends both.

slides.subTitle: Optimizing the wrong metric
slides.markdown: A recommender optimized purely for **click-through rate** learns to promote clickbait — clicks rise while user satisfaction and long-term retention fall. This is **proxy metric divergence**: you can't directly measure the real goal ("is the user happy"), so you optimize a measurable stand-in ("did they click"), and the model happily exploits the gap between the two. The fix isn't a better model — it's choosing a proxy closer to the real goal (e.g. 7-day return rate) and tracking the real metric alongside it, not just the proxy.

slides.subTitle: Data to monitoring, and back
slides.markdown:
Shipping an ML feature is a loop, not a one-time training run:

![The ML lifecycle: data, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor, feeding back into data](assets/ml-lifecycle.svg)

**Data** is collected and labeled, a model is **trained** and **evaluated** offline against held-out data, then **deployed** behind a rollback path, then **monitored** in production for drift — feeding new data back into the next training round.
